Leveraging deep learning applied to chest radiograph images to identify individuals at high risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a retrospective model validation study

Saman Doroodgar Jorshery, Jay Chandra, Anika S Walia, Audra Stumiolo, Kristin Corey, Seyedeh Maryam Zekavat, Aniket N Zinzuwadia, Krisha Patel, Sarah Short, Jessica L Mega, R Scooter Plowman, Neha Pagidipati, Shannon S Sullivan, Kenneth W Mahaffey, Svati H Shah, Adrian F Hernandez, David Christiani, Hugo J W L Aerts, Jakob Weiss, Michael T Lu, Vineet K Raghu, on behalf of the Project Baseline Health Study Group

Summary Background Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a leading cause of mortality, yet early detection remains challenging. This study assessed whether deep learning applied to routine outpatient chest radiographs (CXRs) can identify individuals at high risk of incident COPD.

Methods Using cancer screening trial data, we previously developed a convolutional neural network (CXR-Lung-Risk) to predict lung-related mortality from a CXR image. In this retrospective model validation study, we externally validated whether CXR-Lung-Risk was associated with incident COPD from routine CXRs. We identified outpatients without lung cancer, COPD, or emphysema who had a CXR taken from Jan 1, 2013, to Dec 31, 2014, at Massachusetts General or Brigham and Women’s Hospitals in Boston, MA, USA. The primary outcome was 6-year incident COPD. Discrimination was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) compared with the TargetCOPD clinical risk score. All analyses were stratified by smoking status. A secondary analysis was conducted in the Project Baseline Health Study (PBHS) to test associations between CXR-Lung-Risk with pulmonary function and plasma protein abundance. The PBHS study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT03154346.

Findings The primary analysis consisted of data from 12 550 ever-smokers (mean age 62⋅4 years [SD 6⋅8], 6135 [48⋅9%] male, 6415 [51⋅1%] female) and 15 298 never-smokers (mean age 63⋅0 years [8⋅1], 6550 [42⋅8%] male, 8748 [57⋅2%] female). 1562 (12⋅4%) of 12 550 ever-smokers and 580 (3⋅8%) of 15 298 never-smokers developed COPD within 6 years. CXR-Lung-Risk had additive predictive value beyond the TargetCOPD score for 6-year incident COPD in both eversmokers (CXR-Lung-Risk + TargetCOPD AUC 0⋅73 [95% CI 0⋅72–0⋅74] vs TargetCOPD alone AUC 0⋅66 [0⋅65–0⋅68], p<0⋅0001) and never-smokers (CXR-Lung-Risk + TargetCOPD AUC 0⋅70 [0⋅67–0⋅72] vs TargetCOPD alone AUC 0⋅60 [0⋅57–0⋅62], p<0⋅0001). In secondary analyses of 2097 individuals in the PBHS, CXR-Lung-Risk was associated with worse pulmonary function and with abundance of SCGB3A2 (secretoglobin family 3A member 2) and LYZ (lysozyme), proteins involved in pulmonary physiology.

Interpretation In this external validation, a deep-learning model applied to routine CXR images identified individuals at high risk of incident COPD, beyond known risk factors. Patients at high risk might benefit from diagnostic spirometry and subsequent preventive care.

Introduction Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterised by persistent respiratory symptoms (dyspnoea, cough, phlegm production) due to airway or alveoli abnormalities that cause prolonged, progressive airflow obstruction. 1 COPD is the third leading cause of mortality and carries an estimated burden of US$30 billion annually to the US health-care system. 2 It is incurable; however, early diagnosis and subsequent lifestyle and pharmaceutical interventions improve prognosis. 1,3,4 The key diagnostic criterion for COPD is a post-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1 ) to forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio of 0⋅7 or less as measured by spirometry. 1

Current guidelines do not recommend screening asymptomatic adults for COPD. 5 Instead, targeted case finding using spirometry has been proposed for individuals with a high suspicion of COPD: patients with chronic respiratory symptoms, structural airway abnormalities, and risk factors (eg, smoking). 1 However, spirometry is often unavailable in low-income countries, 6 and it is underutilised with disparate accessibility across sociodemographic groups in high-income countries, 7 leading to estimates that 50–75% of COPD cases remain undiagnosed. 8 Although patients with undiagnosed COPD are typically at an earlier disease stage, 9 these individuals have a similar mortality risk to those with confirmed COPD. 10 Identifying undiagnosed

Current approaches to identify patients at high COPD risk focus on surveys or questionnaires during routine primary care. 11 Another promising approach is to opportunistically identify high-risk individuals using electronic medical record (EMR) data obtained during routine clinical care. Smoking is a major driver of COPD risk, but it is often not documented or is recorded inaccurately in the EMR, 12 and a growing proportion of COPD cases occur in never-smokers, for whom there are fewer well established risk factors. 13

Chest radiographs (CXRs) are one of the most common tests in medicine 14 and a first-line test for respiratory symptoms, including in primary and urgent care. Recent advances in deep learning, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have enabled breakthroughs in extracting information from a CXR image to assess disease risk. 15

We previously developed a CNN called CXR-Lung-Risk that estimates 18-year lung-related mortality risk (including death due to COPD, lung cancer, interstitial lung disease, and chronic emphysema) based on a single posterioranterior CXR image. 16 In multiple clinical trial cohorts, the CXR-Lung-Risk output was associated with lung-related mortality and all-cause mortality in patients with lung cancer. It is not yet known whether the CXR-Lung-Risk score predicts COPD incidence.

In this study, we tested whether CXR-Lung-Risk can be applied to routine, outpatient CXR images to identify patients at high risk of incident COPD. We assessed

whether CXR-Lung-Risk predicts COPD risk better than or complementary to an EMR-based clinical risk score (TargetCOPD). 17 Additionally, we leveraged CXR images from Project Baseline Health Study (PBHS) participants to test whether a high CXR-Lung-Risk score was associated with lung function and plasma protein concentrations.

Methods Study design and cohort We did a retrospective model validation study using outpatient data routinely collected from Mass General Brigham Hospitals (MGB; Massachusetts General and Brigham and Women’s Hospitals) in Boston, MA, USA (figure 1). Our primary analysis included data from outpatients aged 50–80 years who had a posterior-anterior CXR taken at MGB from Jan 1, 2013, to Dec 31, 2014, and no history of lung cancer, COPD, or chronic emphysema as defined by the ICD-9 and ICD-10 diagnosis codes (appendix p 6). Analyses were performed in subcohorts stratified by ever-smokers or never-smokers. This study was approved by the MGB Institutional Review Board (protocol number 2021P000834) with a waiver of informed consent for retrospective analysis of de-identified data. The study followed Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis – Artificial Intelligence (TRIPOD-AI) reporting guidelines. 18 No protocol was prepared for this study.

Research in context

Evidence before this study We searched PubMed for articles related to early detection or risk prediction of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease published in English between database inception and May 3, 2024, using the search terms (((COPD[Title/Abstract]) OR (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease[Title/Abstract])) AND ((Early Detection[Title/ Abstract]) OR (Case Finding[Title/Abstract]) OR (Risk Prediction [Title/Abstract]) OR (Risk Calculator[Title/Abstract]) OR (Risk Estimation[Title/Abstract])) AND (Humans[Filter])) NOT (Lung Cancer[Title/Abstract]) NOT (Systematic Review[Title/ Abstract]). We found 664 articles, of which 56 reported new prediction tools for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Of these, 32 were tools to identify adults with undiagnosed COPD or predict COPD risk—the other 24 were prediction tools for acute exacerbations or mortality risk in those with diagnosed COPD. Of these 32, 28 tools required self-reported symptoms or detailed smoking histories, unlikely to be available in the electronic medical record. Of the remaining four tools, two required chest CT scans. One study showed that deep learning applied to chest radiographs could discriminate between COPD cases and controls; however, this was developed and tested in a small sample (1000 patients), which included individuals receiving chest radiographs as part of a

physical examination in China. The other tool was the TargetCOPD case-finding model, which we use as a comparator in this Article. We previously showed that a deep-learning model called CXR-Lung-Risk could calculate a score in years associated with lung-related mortality using a single chest radiograph image.

Added value of this study In this external validation study of more than 27 000 patients, we applied the CXR-Lung-Risk model to chest radiographs obtained during routine clinical care and found that this score was associated with COPD incidence beyond clinical risk factors. In a secondary analysis, we found that this score was associated with worse pulmonary function and with plasma protein abundances indicative of poorer lung function.

Implications of all the available evidence These findings suggest that there is novel information on chest radiograph images associated with future COPD risk and lung function. As chest radiography is a widely used imaging modality, opportunistic screening of existing chest radiographs using a deep learning-based model (CXR-Lung-Risk) could help identify high-risk individuals and guide COPD prevention.

The deeply phenotyped PBHS cohort consists of 2502 participants enriched for risk factors for lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, who had demographic, survey, clinical, molecular, laboratory, and imaging records taken at the initial study visit. To test the association of CXR-Lung-Risk with pulmonary function, we analysed data from 1263 patients who had posterior-anterior CXR images and pulmonary function testing. To test the association of CXR-Lung-Risk with plasma protein abundance, we analysed data from 957 patients who had CXR imaging and proteomic data available (figure 1). Individuals with known lung cancer or prevalent COPD were removed from all analyses. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials. gov, NCT03154346.

CXR-Lung-Risk and CXR images CXR-Lung-Risk was developed to predict a composite outcome of 18-year mortality due to lung disease (COPD, lung

cancer, interstitial lung disease, chronic emphysema) based on a single CXR image using 147 497 images from the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial. 16 This model was validated in two held-out testing datasets of asymptomatic screening trial participants. Here, we tested whether CXR-Lung-Risk was associated with 6-year COPD incidence in a patient cohort who had CXRs taken during routine care. A summary of the training procedure for CXR-Lung-Risk is available in the appendix (p 3). The output of the model is a score in years such that a score of 60 years means that an individual has lung-related mortality risk equivalent to that of an average individual aged 60 years. We assessed whether this CXR-Lung-Risk score was associated with 6-year COPD incidence.

We externally validated CXR-Lung-Risk using the existing free, open-source version without alterations. Routine CXRs taken from patients at the MGB were obtained from the Picture Archiving and Communication System. For patients with multiple radiographs, we used the earliest radiograph during the study period. Smoking history, risk factors, race, and ethnicity In the MGB cohort, data for smoking history and risk factors, including recent dyspnoea and medication use, were obtained from the EMR. Smoking status was determined through manual review of clinical history, physical examination, and pulmonary function reports. A previously described algorithm 20 was used to extract pack-years at the time of the CXR image for each patient. Patients without any smoking information were considered never-smokers. The presence of COPD and other comorbidities were identified using ICD codes (appendix p 6). 21 Race and ethnicity were based on self-reported data and followed guidelines outlined in the National Institutes of Health Policy on Reporting Race and Ethnicity Data. 22 Sex was defined as the patient’s legal sex, which is sex at birth unless the patient requested to change this. In the PBHS, all risk factors were self-reported.

Outcomes The primary outcome was COPD incidence within 6 years after the CXR based on ICD codes from the EMR (appendix p 6). We chose a 6-year outcome to balance using a long-term outcome versus having sufficient follow-up. In our study, our median follow-up was 7⋅2 (IQR 5⋅4–8⋅0) years in smokers and 7⋅7 (7⋅0–8⋅4) years in never-smokers. All-cause mortality was determined using the Social Security Master Death Index and the MGB death registration system.

TargetCOPD risk score We compared CXR-Lung-Risk with the TargetCOPD score, 17 a regression model that predicts risk of undiagnosed COPD using EMR data including age, smoking status, dyspnoea, prescriptions for a short-acting beta agonist (SABA), and antibiotics prescriptions. TargetCOPD was developed and validated from a large primary care cluster-randomised controlled case-finding trial. 23 For binary analyses, we used the published threshold of a 7⋅5% risk or higher. We assessed whether CXR-Lung-Risk was associated with incident COPD beyond the TargetCOPD score. Patients without medication information were considered to have no prescriptions for salbutamol or antibiotics (0⋅7% of the cohort). Patients with no ICD codes were assumed to not have dyspnoea (1⋅7% of the cohort).

Protein abundance data Plasma proteins from 957 PBHS participant samples were used to associate CXR-Lung-Risk with underlying biological disease mechanisms. Each sample was prepared using microflow high-resolution liquid chromatographymass spectrometry. These raw data were converted to protein abundances using Dia-NN, v1.8.1. The appendix (p 4) shows detailed quality control steps. 289 proteins were detected across all patient plasma samples. Microbial

proteins, contaminants, and immunoglobulin variable chain proteins were excluded.

Saliency maps for explainability We generated saliency maps to better understand which anatomic regions of the radiograph contribute most to the CXR-Lung-Risk output (we wrote the code and implemented it in PyTorch v2.0). For each patient, we calculated an average saliency map across the 20 models in the CXR-Lung-Risk ensemble and superimposed the resulting map on the original radiographs for visualisation.

Statistical analysis We assessed the association of the continuous CXR-Lung- Risk score (in years) and the TargetCOPD score with 6-year, 3-year, and 1-year COPD incidence using the timedependent area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUC) and precision-recall (AUPRC) curves. We used DeLong’s method to calculate confidence intervals. We assessed calibration using the integrated calibration index (ICI). 24 Since neither CXR-Lung-Risk nor TargetCOPD directly predict 6-year COPD risk, we used optimism-corrected bootstrapping 25 with logistic regression to convert each score to 6-year COPD risk to estimate ICI. We conducted all analyses separately in ever-smokers and never-smokers and across sex and race-based subgroups. We used decision curve analysis 26 to assess the net benefit of the CXR-Lung- Risk, TargetCOPD, and baseline strategies of screening all and no patients across realistic risk thresholds.

To address censoring, we assessed the association of the CXR-Lung-Risk score with incident COPD using Cox proportional hazards, adjusted for clinical variables including age, smoking status, recent dyspnoea, SABA use, prevalent asthma, antibiotic use, and findings from the CXR report, including the presence of a lung opacity, atelectasis, pneumothorax, pneumonia, oedema, consolidation, or a lung lesion. We stratified the continuous CXR-Lung-Risk score into three ordinal groups (low risk ≤50; moderate risk >50–≤55; and high risk >55). Cumulative incidence curves were calculated to assess the association of the ordinal risk groups with COPD incidence. All analyses were stratified by ever-smokers versus never-smokers, because COPD aetiology is different in non-smokers. 1 No significant demographic interactions were found in the association of CXR-Lung-Risk with COPD incidence, so these terms were excluded.

Secondary analyses were conducted in PBHS participants with pulmonary function tests and plasma proteomics. We calculated the association of CXR-Lung-Risk with percentage of predicted peak expiratory flow (PEF); percentage of predicted FVC; percentage of predicted FEV 1 , FEV 1 /FVC ratio, percentage of predicted diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO); and abundance of 289 plasma proteins using linear regression adjusted for age, sex, self-reported race, respiratory disease, BMI, and study site. Significant proteins were identified using a Bonferroni-corrected p value lower than 0⋅05 based on a t test. All analyses were stratified by

Results Our primary analysis included data from 27 848 outpatients who had a posterior-anterior CXR taken from Jan 1, 2013, to Dec 31, 2014 (table 1). Of these, 12 550 patients had ever smoked cigarettes (mean age 62⋅4 [SD 6⋅8], 6135 [48⋅9%] male, 6415 [51⋅1%] female, 10 487 [90⋅6%] White), and 15 298 patients had never smoked (mean age 63⋅0 [SD 8⋅1], 6550 [42⋅8%] male, 8748 [57⋅2%] female, 11 748 [85⋅8%] White; table 1). In this cohort, 1562 (12⋅4%) of 12 550 eversmokers and 580 (3⋅8%) of 15 298 never-smokers developed COPD within 6 years. MGB cohort characteristics were similar to those of the CXR-Lung-Risk model development cohort (appendix p 9); however, the smokers in the MGB cohort had a milder smoking history (mean 15⋅9 pack-years [SD 20⋅0]) than did smokers in the CXR-Lung-Risk model development cohort (35⋅5 pack-years [29⋅0]).

We first assessed the association of the continuous CXR- Lung-Risk and TargetCOPD scores with 6-year, 3-year, and 1-year COPD incidence (table 2). We found that a combined model of CXR-Lung-Risk and TargetCOPD had 0⋅08 higher AUC for 6-year COPD incidence than TargetCOPD alone, in the full cohort (CXR-Lung-Risk + TargetCOPD AUC: 0⋅74 [95% CI 0⋅72–0⋅76] vs TargetCOPD AUC: 0⋅66 [0⋅64–0⋅68], p<0⋅0001), 0⋅07 higher AUC among ever-smokers only (0⋅73 [0⋅72–0⋅74] vs 0⋅66 [0⋅65–0⋅68], p<0⋅0001), and 0⋅10 higher AUC among never-smokers only (0⋅70 [0⋅67–0⋅72] vs 0⋅60 [0⋅57–0⋅62], p<0⋅0001; table 2). Similar results were seen for 3-year and 1-year COPD incidence (table 2); subgroup analyses by sex, selfreported race, and Hispanic ethnicity (appendix p 10–11); and when using AUPRC (appendix p 12). Both models were well calibrated, although TargetCOPD slightly underestimated risk in smokers, especially non-White smokers (appendix pp 13, 19). Decision curve analyses showed that the CXR-Lung-Risk score had the highest net benefit across reasonable risk thresholds in smokers (5–20%) and non-smokers (2⋅5–7⋅5%) and similar net benefit to the TargetCOPD score outside this range in non-smokers (appendix p 20).

We next tested the association of ordinal CXR-Lung-Risk categories with incident COPD (appendix p 16). In eversmokers, a graded association with incident COPD was observed across moderate (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 1⋅7 [95% CI 1⋅5–1⋅9]) and high (aHR 3⋅4 [2⋅9–3⋅9]) CXR- Lung-Risk categories compared with the low-risk category, after adjusting for risk factors and radiologist findings on the CXR report (figure 2A). A similar pattern was observed in never-smokers, with a higher risk of incident COPD in the moderate (aHR 1⋅6 [1⋅3–1⋅9]) and high (aHR 2⋅4

[1⋅9–3⋅0]) CXR-Lung-Risk categories compared with the low-risk category after adjustment (figure 2B).

We compared incident COPD rates among patients at high-risk by CXR-Lung-Risk and those at high-risk by TargetCOPD using the published 7⋅5% risk threshold (table 3). 17 We found that patients with high CXR-Lung- Risk score had high rates of 6-year COPD in both eversmokers (23⋅6% [95% CI 22⋅0–25⋅1]) and never-smokers (7⋅8% [6⋅8–8⋅9]). Relatively high rates were also observed for 3-year COPD incidence (ever-smokers: 9⋅9% [8⋅8–11⋅0]; never-smokers: 5⋅6% [4⋅8–6⋅5]) and 1-year COPD incidence (ever-smokers: 2⋅7% [2⋅1–3⋅3]; never-smokers: 3⋅8% [3⋅1– 4⋅6]). CXR-Lung-Risk was complementary to the Target- COPD score, with patients at high risk by both models having a 28⋅4% (26⋅4–30⋅2) and 11⋅5% (8⋅8–14⋅4) rate of 6-year COPD in ever-smokers and never-smokers, respectively. Patients at low risk by both approaches had a 4⋅7% (4⋅1–5⋅5) and 2⋅2% (1⋅9–2⋅5) rate of 6-year COPD in ever-smokers and never-smokers, respectively. Similar results were found for 3-year and 1-year outcomes (appendix p 17).

Every SD in CXR-Lung-Risk (6 years) was associated with a 2⋅4–5⋅3% worse pulmonary function for ever-smokers (p<0⋅05 for all comparisons) after adjustment. Then, we conducted proteomics analysis in 957 participants who had CXR imaging and proteomic data available for 289 plasma proteins. We found that two proteins had a significant positive relationship with CXR-Lung-Risk (Bonferroni-adjusted p value <0⋅05): SCGB3A2 (secretoglobin family 3A member 2) and LYZ (lysozyme; figure 3), which persisted after adjustment for lung or chronic kidney disease history (appendix p 24). In smokers, SFTPB (surfactant protein B) and LRG1 (leucine-rich α-2 glycoprotein 1) were significantly associated with CXR-Lung-Risk, whereas LYZ and SCGB3A2 had similar effect sizes but no significant association with CXR-Lung-Risk (appendix p 24). For neversmokers, LYZ had a similar adjusted effect size as in the full analysis; however, the association of SCGB3A2 and SFTPB with CXR-Lung-Risk was attenuated (appendix p 25).

Discussion Chest radiographs are a first-line test for respiratory symptoms but are non-diagnostic for COPD. We hypothesised that a CNN model, CXR-Lung-Risk, could extract hidden information from the CXR image to identify individuals at high COPD risk. Our major findings were that (1) CXR-Lung-Risk was associated with 6-year incident COPD beyond a clinical risk score in ever-smokers (AUC difference=0⋅07 for combined CXR-Lung-Risk+Target- COPD vs TargetCOPD) and never-smokers (AUC difference=0⋅10); (2) patients with high CXR-Lung-Risk had high rates of 6-year COPD (ever-smokers: 23⋅6%; never-smokers: 7⋅8%); and (3) higher CXR-Lung-Risk was associated with

poor pulmonary function and with plasma proteins related to lung function.

Despite significant advances in diagnostic criteria for COPD, 1 half of COPD cases remain undiagnosed. Potential reasons include inaccessibility of spirometry, lack of public awareness of symptoms, and similar respiratory symptoms in patients with comorbidities. 6 Since persistent respiratory symptoms are required to diagnose COPD, routine screening of asymptomatic adults is not recommended. Instead, targeted case finding via patient surveys or questionnaires or risk factor-based scores might be more effective to identify high-risk individuals likely to be diagnosed with COPD. 5

Our vision for CXR-Lung-Risk is a tool to identify highrisk individuals through opportunistic screening of existing CXRs. Despite its low cost ($28 in USA) 27 and radiation dose (0⋅1 mSv or 10 days of background radiation), we do not recommend CXR solely to assess COPD risk. Instead, the CXR-Lung-Risk model could scan the EMR, estimate risk using CXRs already administered during routine care, and alert providers about high-risk patients (figure 1). process would be relatively inexpensive. Potential next steps for high-risk patients include a respiratory symptom questionnaire, surveillance for signs of COPD, or diagnostic spirometry. In regions where spirometry is unavailable, CXR-Lung-Risk could be applied to routine CXRs performed for other indications (eg, tuberculosis screening) to support COPD case finding. This opportunistic screening could complement low-cost alternatives (eg, case-finding questionnaires) to identify patients.

CXR-Lung-Risk might be recognising signs of undiagnosed COPD, as 2⋅7% and 3⋅8% of ever-smokers and neversmokers, respectively, at high CXR-Lung-Risk had COPD diagnosed within 1 year, suggesting that at most 26–37 individuals need to be screened to detect one undiagnosed COPD case. High-risk smokers and never-smokers according to CXR-Lung-Risk smokers continued to accrue COPD diagnoses over 6 years with a 23⋅6% and 7⋅8% 6-year incidence, respectively. Adding CXR-Lung-Risk to the TargetCOPD score increased the discrimination for 6-year incident COPD in ever-smokers (AUC difference=0⋅07) and never-smokers (AUC difference=0⋅10). This finding suggests that combining the CXR image with risk factors from the medical record might further improve performance.

A concern with deep learning is the lack of interpretability. We previously showed that CXR-Lung-Risk was associated with risk factors including age, sex, obesity, smoking, cardiovascular disease, and emphysema, fibrosis, and lung opacities on the CXR. 16 Here, we used saliency maps to identify regions on the image that most contribute to the CXR-Lung-Risk score. Traditional CXR findings indicative of COPD include upper lung emphysematous changes and lung hyperinflation leading to a small cardiac silhouette. Consistent with these established findings, people with high CXR-Lung-Risk scores had strong activations in the upper lungs and mediastinum. Activations were also consistently noted in the inferior leftward aspect of the aortic knob (the silhouette of the aorta where it arches from the front to the back of the chest), for patients with high and low CXR-Lung-Risk scores. This relationship with COPD is less clear—the aorta becomes tortuous and calcified with age, and this may act as a surrogate for age.

We then leveraged data from PBHS and found strong associations of CXR-Lung-Risk with poor lung function. DLCO and the FEV 1 /FVC ratio were negatively associated with CXR-Lung-Risk, with a stronger effect observed in smokers. DLCO is a marker of many lung diseases and FEV 1 /FVC ratio is a marker of obstructive lung diseases such as COPD and asthma. 1 All pulmonary function tests (PEF, FEV 1 /FVC ratio, and DLCO) were negatively associated with CXR-Lung-Risk in smokers.

Given the potential of plasma proteins as COPD biomarkers, 28 we tested associations between CXR-Lung-Risk and plasma protein concentrations to gain further insight into potential mechanisms. We found positive associations of SCGB3A2 and LYZ concentrations with CXR-Lung-Risk. SCGB3A2 is a cytokine molecule only expressed in the

lungs by the bronchiolar club cells. 29 It is protective against lung disease processes including inflammation, fibrosis, and malignancy. 29 LYZ is an enzyme that primarily degrades bacterial cell walls. It is expressed in the lungs, plasma, stomach, and salivary glands and is overexpressed in the lungs of patients with COPD and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. 30 Additionally, LYZ has been specifically linked to the development of pulmonary emphysema. 31

These analyses suggest that CXR-Lung-Risk may be picking up imaging signs specific to biological pathways of reduced lung function.

Limitations of this study should be considered. First, the primary analysis used patients having routine CXR at a single hospital system in Boston, and most were non-Hispanic White. Although subgroup analysis showed robust performance across self-reported race and ethnicity, future studies must test the model in racially and geographically diverse populations, especially as COPD may have a heterogeneous aetiology across ancestries. 32 Second, CXR- Lung-Risk consists of a CNN ensemble that achieved high performance; however, performance may improve further with modern architectures (eg, vision transformers). 33 Third, risk factors including smoking were ascertained from the EMR. Although, in the USA, smoking status documentation is required by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Meaningful Use regulation, this information may be inaccurate and affect analyses. 13 Fourth, we used CXRs taken from Jan 1, 2013, to Dec 31, 2014, to ensure a 6-year follow-up period, but trends in COPD diagnosis and prevalence might have changed since then. Finally, a criticism of risk prediction models is that they tend to identify older and frailer individuals as high risk; therefore, the impact of CXR-Lung- Risk on early detection must be addressed in a prospective trial.

In conclusion, we externally validated CXR-Lung-Risk, an open-source tool, to identify patients at high COPD risk based on a routine CXR image from the EMR. CXR-Lung- Risk predictions were associated with pulmonary function and with plasma proteins indicative of lung health. Future research will validate CXR-Lung-Risk in diverse populations and examine how to incorporate CXR-Lung-Risk into clinical workflows.
